messages.author: 728018107a130d02
messages.subject: Logistic GP
parts:
Hi all,

I'm testing out a fairly straightforward model. The basic idea is to assess how likely it is someone will purchase on a particular day, given time since last purchase (interpurchase time). Traditionally, hazard models are used for this sort of thing, but I'm testing instead using Gaussian Processes to estimate a latent "propensity to buy" function, where purchases are binary variables modeled as a bernoulli_logit of the propensity. Basically, the data are a string of 1's or 0's, with 1 indicating purchase, and with an associated interpurchase time counter, so a typical section of the data might look like:

P:  0 0 1   |   0 0 0 0 1   |    0 ...
T:  1 2 3   |   1 2 3 4 5   |   1 ...

In my simulations, there are 500 customers, tracked for 50 days. The GP has interpurchase time as its only input, so we're estimating a latent function f(t), where t=1,...,50 (and thus the covariance matrix is 50x50).

In the code attached, I use a parametric form to set this latent function, then try to recover it with a GP specification like done in the stan manual. The first concern is that the model takes forever to run, but this isn't ultimately why I'm posting. The major concern is that, depending on whether or not I estimate the parameters of the covariance function, I get wildly different results.

More specifically, I start by doing a full analysis on everything, estimating both the latent function and the hyperparameters of the covariance function (called "gpp_simple" in the code). Once that estimation finishes running, I take the median of the estimated hyperparameters, then fix the covariance function with those values. I then estimate the GP again (called "gpp_spec2"). The results make little sense:
  • In the full estimation case, I get results that make sense, especially when interpreted on the "probability" scale instead of the latent function scale. The two plots are numbered 1 and 2, attached, where the mean of the estimation is in black, and the truth is in red dotted.
  • In the fixed hyperparameters case, I get nonsense results for about half of the time periods--it starts out looking fine, then goes crazy. These results are numbered 3 and 4, attached, where again the mean of the estimation is in black, and the truth is in red dotted.
So basically, the latent function is recovered in the more uncertain case, where I let stan estimate the hyperparameters, but is not recovered when I fix the hyperparameters at reasonable values (I should add that I've tried a wide range of values--this happens consistently). I'm not an expert in GPs by any means, so it's possible there's something I'm missing theoretically.

One thing to note: as you can tell in the attached graphics, the model works for the first several time periods. It also seems to work if I limit the number of time periods to just that number---say, t.max=20. More than that, though, and it goes crazy. At 50, the problem is most clearly evident. Things get even crazier, though, as t.max gets higher. Typically, I would attribute that to a problem with many inputs, since the time period is the only input to the GP, but it doesn't explain why the model works, regardless of t.max (and slow run time), if I allow estimation of the hyperparameters, instead of fixing them at their (previously estimated) values.

Any help would be much appreciated! Specifically looking to understand why this might be happening--an error in my understand of GPs/stan, or a stan error/quirk of some kind.

Thanks,
Ryan

messages.author: 368f61d9252655a2
messages.subject: Re: Logistic GP
parts:
Looks like numerical instability problem, ie. too small amount of jitter is added to diagonal. Changing the current value 1e-12 to something more reasonable like 1e-4 gives much better fit (attached plots) and sampling is quite a bit faster too.

(This seems to be a common problem with GPs, maybe some notes should be added to the manual?)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Logistic GP
parts:
This is fantastic. Works just like you said.

I didn't realize the jitter would have such an impact on performance. In my original formulation, I didn't even have jitter, since it's a logistic GP, and (I think) noise shouldn't be necessary along the diagonal. I just figured it would improve stability to add a little bit. Guess I didn't add enough!

Thanks for your help.

Yes, in theory jitter is not needed. In practice it may help a lot without changing the model. Radford Neal* writes that a small amount of jitter (e.g. 0.01)  alters the logistic model only slightly. A larger amount of jitter (e.g. 10) will make the model to perform as probit model, and you could even make the amount of jitter to be a hyperparameter.

* Radford Neal. Regression and classification using Gaussian process priors. In Bayesian Statistics 6, Bernardo et al (eds), pp. 475-501, Oxford University Press, 1998.

I'm interested to know how fast your inference is now with the larger amount of jitter?

Aki

torstai 9. huhtikuuta 2015 12.39.30 UTC+3 Aki Vehtari kirjoitti:

I'm interested to know how fast your inference is now with the larger amount of jitter?

Original model ~ 1h, if I remember correctly
801.457 seconds (Total), jitter=1e-4
227.698 seconds (Total), jitter=1e-3
48.9558 seconds (Total), jitter=1e-2
32.0593 seconds (Total), jitter=1e-1
35.1014 seconds (Total), jitter=1e0
66.4915 seconds (Total), jitter=1e1
241.381 seconds (Total), jitter=half-cauchy(0,1)

Of course, thats not the whole story (efficient sample size etc).

Making jitter to be hyperparameter seems to be quite promising approach, pretty good balance between time/quality. Any recommendations for the prior? (half-cauchy probably isn't that good, at least not with that scale).

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Logistic GP
parts:
Thanks Herra Huu!

When thinking possible prior choices for the jitter, the problem is that we are willing to move away from logit model to get faster sampling, and then the choice of prior is not based on our prior knowledge (or lack-of knowledge).

If ignoring the computational speed, it might be helpful to think that probit corresponds to latent Gaussian and logit is close to latent Student-t with nu=7. The model with the jitter hyperparameter will have these as limits.

Aki
